## Biography

Tionisla's annex smells of preservation oils and old metal. That smell clings to Dr Reuben Hale's hands — grey-eyed, thin, permanently smudged with workshop grit — the way chalk dust used to cling to schoolmasters.

Hale curates the Historical Society's most dangerous collection: not the graveyard outside, but the memory of how humanity learned to cheat distance. The Faraway lattice. The Quirium miracle. The collapse of GalCop and the ban on sentient AI that followed, too late, like locking a door after the fire has already walked through. He coined the term "the Missing" for vessels that entered hyperspace and never emerged — a clinical phrase for a haunted statistic. When Jasmina Halsey's auditorium recording matched the cadence of a Quirium Control Unit that had not responded to human contact in two centuries, Hale did not flinch. He documented the chain of custody, packed the unit in non-reactive foam, and handed it to her. "The Missing left traces in witch-space," he said. "Perhaps now is the time to find those ghosts and put them to rest."
